text:
Moth and Gravel Field Note 5. A
green light should mean

something. An AI narrated
edition of the published note.

What exactly is all right? A
green light is wonderfully

efficient. One glance, one small
exhale. The thing is all right.

You can turn your attention
elsewhere. But what exactly is

all right? As we work across our
software pipeline, that small

question keeps returning. A
process is running. A job has

ended. A checked plan has passed
its expected case. Each deserves

a clear answer. Each asks
something different. The color

can travel more easily than the
meaning. Start with the

question. Gaiden is being
developed as a calm workspace

companion. It brings the current
issue, repositories, services,

and evidence into one place. Its
contract makes an important

distinction. A healthy runtime
is an observation about the

runtime. Feature acceptance
needs its own evidence. That

distinction belongs in the
interface. A person should be

able to see a service running
without having to infer that the

intended work has been verified.
The contract also keeps a failed

runtime probe unknown. An
observation that did not succeed

cannot establish that an
application stopped. This is a

small wording problem with a
large consequence. The interface

has to leave room for what it
could not learn.

O1, observation. Is it running?
A runtime observation answers a

question about the service's
present state. O2, expectation.

Did the case behave as expected?
A case can pass by correctly

refusing unsafe step or
preserving an unknown outcome.

O3, evidence. Is the result
established? Delivery needs

evidence of its own. Missing
observations remain visible.

Three questions to keep
distinct. Explanatory drawings,

not screenshots, or proposed
shared product interface. The

labels summarize the documented
boundaries described in this

note. A passing case can
preserve a question. A Yedo

checks agent plans and records
their execution. Its local

integration report contains a
useful wrinkle. Every acceptance

case in the final run passed
while the delivery records still

included incomplete, unknown,
and unresolved outcomes. Those

outcomes can be correct. A case
designed to refuse an unsafe

next step passes when the
refusal holds. A case designed

to preserve a lost
acknowledgment passes when the

missing answer remains missing.
The local integration report

records six verified delivery
sub-probes separately from its

34 passing cases. The
distinction is the story. It

lets a reviewer understand both
the mechanism's behavior and the

work actually established. These
are different boundary fixtures,

not a sample from which to
calculate a general success

rate. A tidy summary must give
the reader a way back to that

difference. The boundary can be
modest. Parja, a build tool for

spare machines, gives green a
narrow job. Every configured

step exited with zero. Its
result file records step

outcomes and typed statuses
distinguish a failed step, an

infrastructure failure,
cancellation, and timeouts. That

is a useful boundary because it
can be explained. The person can

inspect the recipe and decide
whether its steps answer the

question they care about. The
color does not have to carry an

unspoken claim about every
possible property of the

software. It also matters where
the verdict comes from. Parja

uses the recorded result and
exit codes rather than

discovering success in an
encouraging sentence buried in a

log. Give uncertainty a place of
its own. So does a refusal that

prevented a mistaken action.
Neither should require a person

to guess whether the tool has
lost track of the work. Across

these projects, the question is
becoming more specific. What can

this indicator honestly let
someone stop worrying about?

That is the promise a green
light should keep. You have been

listening to Moth and Gravel
Field Notes. The written edition
is at mothandgravel.com.
